title_or_table: Title 28, sections 1, 41, 44, 81 to 131 and 133, and Title 48, sections 1424, 1424b, 1611, 1614 and 1821: the federal courts and their authorized judgeships

universe_or_base: The Supreme Court, the 13 courts of appeals, the 91 district courts of the states, DC and Puerto Rico, and the 3 territorial district courts
unit: courts; judgeships authorized by statute (not judges serving: vacancies and senior judges are not counted)
vintage: United States Code, 2024 edition, on govinfo.gov
qualification: Authorized judgeships are seats the law creates, not judges in office; a later law changing a count would not be in the 2024 edition. The Federal Circuit hears appeals by subject (patents and some federal claims) from every district. 28 U.S.C. 41 still lists the District of the Canal Zone in the Fifth Circuit; it has no court today and is left out.

printed_source_line: Source: U.S. Code, Title 28, sections 1, 41, 44, 81 to 131 and 133, and Title 48, sections 1424b, 1614 and 1821, 2024 edition, United States and territories. Retrieved November 12, 2026. Judgeships the law authorizes, not judges serving.
domain_note: V7’s "Courts" subsystem: how courts are staffed and run
notes: Courts of appeals judgeships: 179; district judgeships of the states, DC and Puerto Rico, shared seats included: 673; territorial: 4.
The territorial courts are not Article III courts: their judges serve ten-year terms (48 U.S.C. 1424b(a), 1614(a), 1821(b)(1)).

The courts count 677 district positions on September 30, 2025 (Judicial Business 2025, Table 10): this file’s 673 statute judgeships and its 4 territorial ones, court by court as the Administrative Office’s table of authorized district judgeships lists them (read November 13, 2026). uscode-federal-trial-judges prints the same account.
